Getting started with Applr

Source: vignettes/Applr.Rmd
Applr.Rmd

A fitted linear model with more than one predictor lives in more dimensions than a scatterplot can show. The usual workaround, geom_smooth(method = "lm"), quietly fits a different, simpler model to the plotted variables, so the line on the screen is not the model you summarized.

Applr draws the model you actually fit. Its core idea is the slice: hold every predictor except one at a fixed value, and draw the model’s predictions as that one predictor varies. Start by fitting an lm(), then hand it to Applr. Explore it with autoplot(), or present it with polish and fine-grained control using geom_slice().

library(Applr)
library(ggplot2)

Explore with autoplot()

autoplot() on an lm builds the whole plot in one call: the model’s own data as a scatter, a fitted slice line with its confidence ribbon, and a subtitle saying what the model is. It also prints summary() to the console, so you can refit, re-plot, and read the coefficients and R² in one step (turn this off with summary = FALSE).

autoplot(lm(Petal.Length ~ Sepal.Length + I(Sepal.Length^2):Species, iris))
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = Petal.Length ~ Sepal.Length + I(Sepal.Length^2):Species, 
#>     data = iris)
#> 
#> Residuals:
#>      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
#> -0.72665 -0.15039  0.00562  0.16639  0.76639 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>                                     Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)                         -3.79412    1.09932  -3.451 0.000731 ***
#> Sepal.Length                         2.04477    0.36389   5.619 9.51e-08 ***
#> I(Sepal.Length^2):Speciessetosa     -0.19763    0.02958  -6.680 4.75e-10 ***
#> I(Sepal.Length^2):Speciesversicolor -0.11503    0.03033  -3.793 0.000218 ***
#> I(Sepal.Length^2):Speciesvirginica  -0.09427    0.02987  -3.156 0.001944 ** 
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Residual standard error: 0.262 on 145 degrees of freedom
#> Multiple R-squared:  0.9786, Adjusted R-squared:  0.978 
#> F-statistic:  1655 on 4 and 145 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
#> Coloured the plot by `Species` - one slice line per level.
#>     To choose the colour, use 'mapping = aes(color = ...)'.

autoplot() makes a few decisions for you. The model’s first numeric predictor goes on the x-axis, and predictors that group into a few discrete values become color, then facets. Every decision can be overridden. Pass a mapping to change the defaults, just as you would with ggplot(); whatever you leave out is still inferred. Choose a different x-axis with aes(x = ...). Arguments in ... pass through to geom_slice(), so interval = "prediction" gives the wider ribbon and interval = "none" a bare line.

model <- lm(hwy ~ displ + drv + cyl, data = mpg)

autoplot(model, aes(color = factor(cyl))) + facet_wrap(~drv)
#> Faceted the plot by `drv` - one panel per level.
#>     For a single panel, drop `drv` from the model.


autoplot(model,
         aes(x = cyl, color = factor(drv)),
         interval = "none") +
  labs(title = "The Same Model From a Different Angle")
#> Value for `displ` not specified - Used mean: 3.472
#>     To choose a slice, use 'predict_vars = list(displ = 3.472)'.

The result is an ordinary ggplot, so + works as usual.

Present with geom_slice()

geom_slice() is the layer underneath autoplot(). It looks like geom_smooth(), but where geom_smooth() fits its own model to the plotted data, geom_slice() draws the model you fitted, reading the plot’s aes() to learn which predictor is on the x-axis. Unlike autoplot(), it makes as few decisions as it can.

Once a model has more than one predictor, each line is a 2-D slice through it. Every predictor not on the x-axis has to be held at some value, and geom_slice() fills those values in this order:

  • Variables named in predict_vars are held at your chosen values.
  • Variables mapped to a grouping aesthetic (aes(color = g)) are held at each group’s value, giving one line per group.
  • Facet variables are held at each panel’s value.
  • Anything left over is imputed (mean for numeric, most common value for factors), with a console message naming the value used.

The model below has four predictors and was fitted exactly, with no noise. A bare geom_slice() has to impute three of them, and the console messages report each choice:

set.seed(123)
n <- 80
x <- runif(n, 0.1, 10)
x2 <- runif(n, 0.1, 10)
x3 <- sample(c(1, 20, 40), n, replace = TRUE)
x4 <- sample(c(1, 2), n, replace = TRUE)
y <- log(5 + x + x2 + x3 + 1/5 * x * x3 + 80 * x4) # no random noise
dat <- data.frame(x, x2, x3, x4, y)

model <- lm(exp(y) ~ x*x3 + x2 + x4, data = dat)   # exact model fit

ggplot(dat, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_slice(model) +
  labs(title = "A Perfectly Fit Model 'Slice'")
#> Value for `x3` not specified - Used mean: 19.36
#>     To choose a slice, use 'predict_vars = list(x3 = 19.36)'.
#> Value for `x2` not specified - Used mean: 4.981
#>     To choose a slice, use 'predict_vars = list(x2 = 4.981)'.
#> Value for `x4` not specified - Used mean: 1.412
#>     To choose a slice, use 'predict_vars = list(x4 = 1.412)'.
#> Predictions of `exp(y)` were back-transformed to match the `y` axis.
#>     To turn this off, use 'back_transform = FALSE'.

# The same model against its full linear predictor: an exact fit
ggplot(dat, aes(x = log(5 + x + x2 + x3 + 1/5 * x * x3 + 80 * x4), y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_slice(model) +
  labs(title = "Same Model, Different X-Axis")
#> Predictions of `exp(y)` were back-transformed to match the `y` axis.
#>     To turn this off, use 'back_transform = FALSE'.

Notice that the response exp(y) was back-transformed onto the plotted y axis without being asked. Those imputations were forced, but you can do better. Map x3 to color, facet by x4, and show the reach of x2 as a band, and every line lands on its points:

ggplot(dat, aes(x, y, color = factor(x3))) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_slice(model, band = "x2", predict_vars = list(x2 = c(0, 10))) +
  facet_wrap(~x4) +
  geom_slice_text() +
  geom_slice_subtitle()
#> Predictions of `exp(y)` were back-transformed to match the `y` axis.
#>     To turn this off, use 'back_transform = FALSE'.

The rest of this vignette goes through those features one at a time.

Choosing slices with predict_vars

Give a variable several values in predict_vars to draw one line per value. Several multi-value variables are crossed.

model <- lm(Sepal.Length ~ Sepal.Width + Petal.Length, iris)

ggplot(iris, aes(Petal.Length, Sepal.Length)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_slice(
    model,
    predict_vars = list(Sepal.Width = c(2, 3, 4)),
    interval = "confidence"
  ) +
  geom_slice_text()

Confidence and prediction intervals

interval = "confidence" or "prediction" shades the corresponding predict.lm() interval around each line:

model <- lm(hwy ~ displ + I(displ^2), data = mpg)

ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_slice(model, interval = "confidence") +
  labs(title = "Confidence Interval")

ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_slice(model, interval = "prediction") +
  labs(title = "Prediction Interval")

Projection bands

An interval shows uncertainty. A band shows the reach of a predictor: two edge slices with a translucent ribbon between them. band = "variable" spans that predictor between the values given in predict_vars, or across its observed range if predict_vars doesn’t mention it. band = TRUE infers the variable when there is only one sensible choice.

model <- lm(hwy ~ displ * drv + cyl, data = mpg)

# Inferred: cyl is the only predictor not shown, so it spans 4 to 8
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_slice(model, band = TRUE) +
  geom_slice_text()
#> Band range for `cyl` not specified - used the min/max data range: 4 to 8.
#>     To choose the range, use 'predict_vars = list(cyl = c(4, 8))'.


# Specified: cyl from 5 to 7
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_slice(model, band = "cyl", predict_vars = list(cyl = c(5, 7))) +
  geom_slice_text()

band cannot be combined with interval.

Transformed responses

If the model’s response is transformed but the plot shows something else, predictions are back-transformed to match the y-axis, and a console message says so. Turn this off with back_transform = FALSE, or pass a function or name (exp, "log10", …) to override the auto-detection.

model <- lm(log(mpg) ~ disp + hp, data = mtcars)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_slice(model) +
  labs(title = "normal y axis")
#> Value for `hp` not specified - Used mean: 146.7
#>     To choose a slice, use 'predict_vars = list(hp = 146.7)'.
#> Predictions of `log(mpg)` were back-transformed to match the `mpg` axis.
#>     To turn this off, use 'back_transform = FALSE'.

ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, log(mpg))) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_slice(model) +
  labs(title = "log() y axis")
#> Value for `hp` not specified - Used mean: 146.7
#>     To choose a slice, use 'predict_vars = list(hp = 146.7)'.

ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_slice(model) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "scale_y_log10() axis")
#> Value for `hp` not specified - Used mean: 146.7
#>     To choose a slice, use 'predict_vars = list(hp = 146.7)'.
#> Predictions of `log(mpg)` were back-transformed to match the `mpg` axis.
#>     To turn this off, use 'back_transform = FALSE'.

Grouping: one line per group

With a grouping aesthetic, each group gets its own slice, and each line stops at the end of its group’s data. full_range = TRUE extends every line across the whole panel instead, like fullrange in geom_smooth():

model <- lm(hwy ~ displ + I(displ^2) + displ:drv, data = mpg)

ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_slice(model)

ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_slice(model, full_range = TRUE)

Labeling the slices

Three companion layers describe the slices on the plot itself, so a reader can tell which line is which and what was held constant. They take no model; they read everything from the plot’s geom_slice() layers, so add them after those layers.

geom_slice_text() labels the end of each line with the values that define it. It is most useful with bands and multi-value predict_vars:

set.seed(123)
n <- 80
x <- runif(n, -10, 10)
x2 <- runif(n, 0, 4)
g <- factor(sample(c("A", "B"), n, replace = TRUE))
y <- x * ifelse(g == "A", 0.5, 2) + ifelse(g == "A", 5, -5) + 4 * x2 + rnorm(n)
dat <- data.frame(x, x2, g, y)
model <- lm(y ~ x * g + x2, data = dat)

ggplot(dat, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_slice(model, predict_vars = list(x2 = c(0, 2, 4), g = c("A", "B"))) +
  geom_slice_text(style = "legend")

geom_slice_subtitle() (or geom_slice_caption()) writes the model equation and any held values that aren’t already shown by the legend, facets, or geom_slice_text(). It indents the equation when there’s room and compresses it when space is tight.

model <- lm(Petal.Length ~ Sepal.Length + I(Sepal.Length^2):Species + Sepal.Width, iris)

ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, Petal.Length, color = Species)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_slice(model, interval = "confidence") +
  geom_slice_subtitle()
#> Value for `Sepal.Width` not specified - Used mean: 3.057
#>     To choose a slice, use 'predict_vars = list(Sepal.Width = 3.057)'.

Where to go next

  • ?geom_slice documents every option, including n, the number of points that make up each line.
  • ?geom_slice_text and ?geom_slice_subtitle cover label styles, placement, and prepend/append text.
  • ?slice_2d and ?add_slice_2d draw the same slices in base graphics.
  • ?scatter_3d (or autoplot(model, type = "3d")) shows a model with two numeric predictors as an interactive 3-D surface.
  • ?lm_equation and ?lm_latex turn the fitted model into text or LaTeX for reports, and ?diagnose draws the standard residual plots.
